Wealth is solid middle class; agriculture is grassland/dairy and cereals, but the tidy suburban-style plots suggest residents commute to a nearby town. German-speaking Catholic Alpine-foreland culture.

Agriculture is grassland/meadow based with small parcels — dairy/forestry mix rather than large collectivized cereal blocks — and household income clearly comes largely from commuting to a nearby district town. Waste is separated per household into paper/glass/residual bins with a domestic composter, an EU-style separated-collection regime.

correction.summary: Austria and Upper Austria were both correct; only the intra-province placement drifted ~70 km, because the analyst leaned on "Mühlviertel granite plateau" while the truth is the Hausruckviertel, the Alpine-foreland hill country south of the Danube. The decisive country-level cues (deep-coloured render with white reveals and under-house garages, per-household wheeled bins with German labels, yellow blade waymarker, unmarked hamlet lanes) were read correctly, and Czechia/Germany/Switzerland were properly excluded. The finer Mühlviertel-vs-Hausruck call was not resolvable from these images; the analyst's own admission of soft confidence was appropriate, but the faint distant high-ridge silhouette in image 1 and the strongly rolling, deeply incised grass-and-stubble relief point south of the Danube rather than to the flat granite plateau.

misleading_cues.observation: Fresh larch board cladding on a new build read as a 'Mühlviertel contemporary vernacular' marker.
misleading_cues.why_misleading: Larch-clad upper storeys on rendered bases are generic across the whole Austrian Alpine foreland and carry no sub-provincial signal.

misleading_cues.observation: Absence of dense Mostbirnbaum orchard rows taken as evidence against the southern Upper Austrian hill country.
misleading_cues.why_misleading: Dense pear-orchard meadows are typical of the Mostviertel/eastern belt; their absence does not push a scene north of the Danube, and the Hausruck has scattered single fruit trees exactly as seen.

misleading_cues.observation: Beech-dominant autumn ridge colour interpreted as granite-plateau (Mühlviertel) forest.
misleading_cues.why_misleading: Mixed beech-spruce ridge forest is equally the norm on the Hausruck and Kobernaußerwald molasse hills; it is not diagnostic of the Bohemian Massif.

decisive_cues.observation: Strongly undulating terrain with short steep grass slopes, incised hollows and forested rounded crests, fields rising directly behind each plot
decisive_cues.why_decisive: Molasse/Hausruck foreland relief is more dissected and steeper-sided than the broad, flat-topped granite plateau of the Mühlviertel.

discriminators.title: Hausruck molasse hills vs Mühlviertel granite plateau in Upper Austria
discriminators.body: In the Hausruckviertel the land is a set of short, steep, deeply dissected grass ridges with rounded beech-spruce crests and views that can catch a hazy Alpine line to the south. In the Mühlviertel you would instead see broad flat-topped plateau surfaces, frequent exposed granite boulders and drystone-granite plinths, more spruce monoculture and no southern high-ridge horizon. Uniform smooth render with no granite stonework, as here, argues against the Bohemian Massif.

discriminators.title: Austrian per-household wheeled bins vs Czech igloo cluster
discriminators.body: In Austrian hamlets each household lines up its own 120–240 L wheeled bins (grey residual/paper, black with a coloured lid) at the driveway apron, often beside a plastic garden composter. In a Czech village you would instead find a shared cluster of fibreglass dome igloos with Czech stream names and EKO-KOM stickers, usually behind mesh fencing at the lane junction.

discriminators.title: Austrian Einfamilienhaus render palette vs German rural render
discriminators.body: Austrian post-1980 rural houses commonly carry saturated single-colour render (deep red, ochre, yellow) with crisp white window reveals and a dark plinth band, with garages recessed under the living floor on a slope. In German villages you would more often see white or pale-grey render with dark-red tiles and free-standing or side-attached garages rather than the sunken under-house garage.

discriminators.title: Yellow blade waymarkers and unmarked Güterwege vs Swiss road furniture
discriminators.body: Austrian rural lanes are unmarked, kerbless asphalt with small yellow directional blade signs at field edges and few other signs. In Switzerland you would instead see dense signage clusters, white-on-blue or yellow Wanderwege plates with distance-in-hours, granite kerbing and frequent white edge lines even on minor roads.
